summary: Keanu, **Massie plans to force a Hegseth impeachment vote** when the House returns Monday, and Fox News reports that several Republicans think it could pass while most will oppose it (Fox News, Washington Examiner). NBC projects Democrats won both chambers, and conservatives are split between blaming the Iran war and tariffs (NBC News, Fox News, The Dispatch). Analysts see **an 80% chance of renewed US-Iran fighting** by Rapidan Energy's estimate, with a third carrier group on the way (CNBC). The Nasdaq rose 1.09% Friday after Thursday's 5.52% drop, and **Anthropic's IPO valuation hopes are falling** toward $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion (CNBC, Axios). In Ukraine, 53 people died in a Russian strike on an aid center ahead of Abu Dhabi talks Nov. 10-11 (CNN, Fox News). Closer to home, **California prosecutors are preparing court challenges** to Newsom's 548 commutations (CalMatters, SF Chronicle), and BART picked developers for 643 homes at Fremont Station (SF Chronicle). It is mild in Fremont this weekend, with highs in the 70s and almost no rain.

stories.title: Massie plans to force a Hegseth impeachment vote when the House returns Nov. 9
stories.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie says he will use a privileged resolution to force a vote on Defense Secretary Hegseth, and Republicans disagree on whether it can pass.
story: Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, told Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to resign or face impeachment as the House returns on Nov. 9, according to the Washington Examiner and Fox News. Massie plans to use a privileged resolution, which forces the House to take it up within two legislative days. His articles accuse Hegseth of abusing his powers in running the Iran war.

Massie first filed the articles in September. The House then left on an early recess, and Massie says leaders did it to dodge the vote. Speaker Mike Johnson denied that and has called the effort a publicity stunt (Fox News, The Hill). Massie lost his primary to a challenger Trump backed. Democrats have their own impeachment articles against Hegseth and say he will be a focus of the new Congress.

The math is disputed. Fox News reports that several House Republicans think the resolution could pass, since a handful of absences could be enough if all Democrats vote yes. Fox also reports that most Republicans will still oppose it, and one lawmaker doubted members would defy a president who is leaving the lame-duck session in a weakened state. Republicans can try a motion to table, which Massie says might have succeeded earlier.

Trump said Wednesday, "I think he's doing a very good job," when asked about replacing Hegseth. A White House official suggested Trump might hold Hegseth accountable during the lame-duck session, per Fox News. Vance and others have blamed the Iran war for the midterm losses, which is why Hegseth's standing has become a test of how far Republicans will break with the president.
stories.flag: No Republican has publicly committed to voting yes, and no vote count exists yet. Predictions of passage rest on unnamed GOP sources.
stories.blindspot: Found mostly right-leaning and center outlets covering this fight; no left-leaning article on the Nov. 9 vote turned up in this pass.
facts: The House returns Monday, Nov. 9.
Massie's resolution is privileged, so the House must act within two legislative days.
Johnson calls the effort a publicity stunt.
Trump said Wednesday he thinks Hegseth is doing a very good job.
Democrats have separate impeachment articles against Hegseth.
stories.left: The Iran war was launched without a clear mandate, and Hegseth ran it. Voters just handed Democrats both chambers partly over that war, and impeachment is the Constitution's tool for a cabinet officer accused of abusing power. Democrats say it should not take a Republican defector to force accountability, and they plan subpoenas and oversight in January regardless.
stories.right: Impeachment is a drastic remedy, and Massie's move looks like personal score-settling after a lost primary. Many conservatives argue that a wartime Pentagon chief should be judged on results and by the president who appointed him, not removed in a lame-duck stunt. Critics inside the party who want Hegseth gone are better served by pressing Trump to replace him than by handing Democrats a victory.
stories.next: The House returns Monday, Nov. 9. Watch for a motion to table and for how many Republicans cross the aisle.

stories.title: Republicans argue over whether the Iran war or tariffs sank them in the midterms
stories.summary: NBC projects Democrats won both chambers, and conservatives are split between blaming the Iran war, tariffs and corruption.
story: NBC News projects that Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms. NBC's House estimates range from about 255 to 259 Democratic seats, well past the 218 needed. Hakeem Jeffries has launched his bid for speaker with no challenger so far. His letter to colleagues lists reversing Medicaid cuts, restoring SNAP funding, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, ending the Trump tariffs and stopping the Iran war.

Republicans are now arguing about why they lost. Vice President JD Vance said, "The reason we lost is the war," and Trump said the war was a major factor but worth it, according to Fox News. Former Sen. Pat Toomey and Sen. Ted Cruz pointed to tariffs as well as the war (Fox News). Fox's own power rankings named both as drivers of defections.

Conservative writers disagree sharply. The Dispatch's Phillip Magness argues the war and gas prices hurt but tariffs were the real millstone. National Review's exit-poll analysis and its editors point to economic frustration, tariffs, corruption allegations around crypto ventures, foreign gifts and pardons, and worries that AI weakens the party's working-class coalition. Ari Fleischer argued the mixed messaging on ending the fighting was the problem.

NBC adds a caution for Democrats. They won on affordability, and delivering it is harder, since Trump has said he will veto what Democrats pass. Democrats are not sworn in until January, so the new majority has little power before then.
facts: NBC News projects Democrats won both the House and the Senate.
NBC's House estimates range from about 255 to 259 Democratic seats.
Jeffries has formally launched his bid for speaker.
Vance blamed the Iran war; Toomey, Cruz and Magness cited tariffs.
The new Congress is sworn in in January.
stories.left: Voters rejected a war they did not ask for and prices that kept rising under tariffs. Democrats read the result as a mandate on affordability, health care and ending the Iran war, and Jeffries has said voters do not want retribution. The strongest version of this view says the party now has to deliver cost relief quickly or risk the same backlash in 2028.
stories.right: The loss reflects a governing record that voters punished, and conservatives who care about the party's future should say so plainly. The strongest right-leaning arguments say tariffs and the war broke the affordability promise, and that corruption stories gave swing voters an easy reason to leave. Many writers also warn that Democrats overread their mandate and that Republicans should rebuild around governance, not grievance.
stories.next: Watch the lame-duck session for veto threats and the first Democratic leadership votes in January.

stories.title: California prosecutors prepare legal challenges to Newsom's death row commutations
stories.summary: Prosecutors say the governor cannot abolish the death penalty by commutation, and a legal group plans to go to the state Supreme Court.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted all 548 California death sentences, and prosecutors across the state are pushing back, according to the San Francisco Chronicle, KQED, CalMatters and Fox News. Orange County DA Todd Spitzer called it "mercy for the wolves," and San Joaquin DA Ron Freitas called it a slap in the face to victims and their families.

Several DAs argue the move substitutes one statewide decision for hundreds of individual jury verdicts. LA County DA Nathan Hochman acknowledged the governor's commutation power but said it does not reach eliminating the death penalty, which only the Legislature or voters can do. San Bernardino DA Jason Anderson said he knew of no victims' families who got notice.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, led by former prosecutor Anne Marie Schubert, pledged to challenge the commutations in the state Supreme Court, and San Diego DA Summer Stephan said her office is researching remedies. The Associated Press reported that 382 of the cases need approval from at least four justices of the California Supreme Court.

Newsom's office says the affected prisoners will stay in prison and are not eligible for release. Spitzer countered that parole rules could move some of them closer to release. CalMatters also looked at what the decision means nationally for the death penalty debate.
facts: Newsom commuted all 548 California death sentences.
Earlier reports cited 563 inmates; the final announcement covered 548.
The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation plans a state Supreme Court challenge.
382 cases still require approval from four state Supreme Court justices, per AP.
Newsom's office says the prisoners are not eligible for release.
stories.left: California has not executed anyone in years, and the death penalty is applied unevenly by race and income. Supporters say a governor's clemency power exists for exactly this, and that ending a system that cost billions without delivering executions is responsible government. Victims' families deserve notice and support, they add, but a sentence nobody carries out helps no one.
stories.right: Voters upheld the death penalty at the ballot, and juries imposed these sentences. Critics say a blanket commutation overrides that choice without a law or a vote, ignores individual cases, and leaves victims' families blindsided. Even people who doubt the death penalty argue that a governor on his way out should not decide it alone.
stories.next: Watch for a petition from the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation in the California Supreme Court.

stories.title: BART picks developers for 643 homes at Fremont Station
stories.summary: The plan would turn BART parking lots into a downtown core Fremont has never had, with approvals hoped for in 2027.
story: The BART board picked Pacific Development and Affirmed Housing in October to negotiate first-phase development at Fremont Station, according to BART and the San Francisco Chronicle. The preliminary plan has 643 homes, 176 of them affordable, on roughly 12 acres of surface parking.

BART's project page also lists a plaza at the station entrance, new bike and pedestrian access from Mowry Avenue and a neighborhood cafe with play and art space. The developers hope for approvals in 2027 and construction starting in 2028, and the project is still early (BART, Traded).

The Chronicle describes Fremont as a city with plenty of jobs but no real downtown. Manufacturing jobs have more than doubled from about 30,000 to 65,000 since 2018, and about 35% of the city's jobs are in manufacturing, per the city. The first five downtown housing complexes have opened, with about 1,000 homes along or near Capitol Avenue. A city economic development official said Fremont is building a downtown from scratch.

The Chronicle notes the BART station opened in 1972 and a city center never formed around it. The city's economic development head argues that workforce and affordable housing on the lots will support retail.
facts: The plan has 643 homes, including 176 affordable.
It covers about 12 acres of BART-owned parking lots.
Developers hope for approvals in 2027 and construction in 2028.
Manufacturing jobs rose from about 30,000 to 65,000 since 2018.
The BART board acted in October 2026.
stories.left: Putting housing on transit parking lots is the clearest way to add homes near jobs and reduce driving. The strongest argument is that 176 affordable units next to BART help workers who now commute in, and that a downtown makes the station more useful. Supporters want the timeline compressed so homes arrive sooner.
stories.right: Housing and transit land should be developed, but critics ask whether 2028 construction and a limited share of affordable units will deliver relief at a reasonable cost. Some conservatives prefer fewer subsidies and fewer requirements so private builders can add more homes faster. They also ask about parking and traffic effects for existing residents.
stories.next: Watch for BART's negotiating agreement terms and city planning hearings, with approvals targeted for 2027.

stories.title: Death toll reaches 53 at Zaporizhzhia aid site as Trump floats a European security deal
stories.summary: US-led Russia-Ukraine talks are set for Abu Dhabi Nov. 10-11, while Europeans question Trump's vague security proposal.
story: Local authorities say 53 people died in a Russian bombing of an aid center in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, CNN reports. Zelensky called it one of the deadliest attacks of the war. NPR's earlier update put the toll at 29 with 48 missing. Officials said KAB-500 and FAB-3000 bombs were used, and at least four police officers were among the dead.
The site was a former school used as a shelter and humanitarian hub. Zelensky said the strike came just before Russia launched a large barrage of drones and missiles at Ukraine's energy system (CNN).

On diplomacy, Steve Witkoff said the US will mediate working-level talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11 on post-war security, de-escalation and humanitarian issues (Fox News). On Thursday Trump teased a "big, beautiful" European security deal after meeting Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, offering few details. Three European officials told CNN they did not know what Trump or Jared Kushner meant, and Zelensky said a Russia-Europe deal could be dangerous.
Putin reportedly still demands the whole Donbas, a smaller Ukrainian military and no NATO path. CNN's analysis argues the new offer may only encourage Putin to escalate.
stories.flag: The terms of Trump's proposed European security deal have not been published; accounts rely on Trump and Kushner's public remarks.
facts: The death toll at the Komyshuvakha aid site reached 53, per local authorities.
US-mediated talks are scheduled for Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11.
Trump teased a 'big, beautiful' European security deal on Thursday.
European officials told CNN they did not know its details.
Putin reportedly still demands all of Donbas.
stories.left: A US president who courts Putin's envoy while Russia kills civilians sends the wrong signal. Critics argue that talks without Ukrainian and European input weaken Kyiv, and that Russia has not shown it wants peace. They want more air defense and tougher sanctions before concessions.
stories.right: Years of war have shown that arming Ukraine alone will not end it, and the talks are a realistic attempt to stop the killing. Conservatives backing Trump argue Europe should carry more of its own security burden, and that US pressure on both sides is the only way to a settlement. Hawks counter that rewarding Russian strikes with talks is a mistake.
stories.next: Watch the Abu Dhabi talks Nov. 10-11 and any text of the security proposal.

stories.title: Analysts see high risk of renewed US-Iran fighting despite the Democratic sweep
stories.summary: A third US carrier group is headed to the region as oil falls on hopes of diplomacy that analysts doubt.
story: CNBC reports that analysts still see a high risk of renewed US-Iran fighting even after Democrats won Congress. Rapidan Energy's Bob McNally put the odds of renewed fighting at 80% and expects Brent and WTI to return above $100 a barrel. Eurasia Group trimmed its estimate of renewed US strikes to 60% from 65% and cut its deal odds to 10% from 20%.

Several tankers have been attacked near Oman since the election, and a third US carrier strike group is heading to the region, CNBC says. Trump said he will decide soon whether to attack again. Fox News reported US "defensive" strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island earlier this week, and Trump called the conflict a "very soft war."

On diplomacy, Iran reportedly sent a nuclear proposal through Qatar, but says it will discuss it only after Washington meets its demands (CNBC). WTI crude ended Friday at $90.83, according to live market data, after falling sharply on Nov. 4 when Vance said the war caused the Republican losses.
Democrats cannot act until January, and Trump could veto a war powers resolution anyway, CNBC notes.
stories.flag: The 80% figure is one analyst's estimate, and Eurasia Group's figures date from a Nov. 5 report.
facts: Rapidan's McNally puts the odds of renewed fighting at 80%.
Eurasia Group puts renewed US strikes at 60% and a deal at 10%.
A third US carrier strike group is heading to the region.
Iran sent a nuclear proposal through Qatar, per reports.
WTI closed at $90.83 on Friday.
stories.left: The war has cost lives, money and a price spike, and voters said so. Democrats want Congress to force an exit through war powers votes and funding limits, and say Trump should take the Qatar channel seriously. They warn that another round of strikes would ignore the election result.
stories.right: Iran cannot be allowed a nuclear weapon, and pressure is what brought Tehran to propose talks. Conservatives who back Trump say a deal needs enforceable terms, and retreating now would reward the regime and Hormuz harassment. Skeptics inside the party worry about costs but still want a strong position.
stories.next: Watch for Trump's decision on new strikes and any response to the Qatari channel.

stories.title: Nasdaq rebounds 1.09% after its worst day since April 2025, but analysts expect more volatility
stories.summary: Chips led Friday's bounce, the Dow slipped, and traders now eye Fed hike odds and next week's inflation data.
story: The Nasdaq rose 1.09% to 24,579.42 on Friday, and the S&P 500 gained 0.31% to 7,376.86, while the Dow fell 0.46% to 51,285.73. The bounce followed Thursday, when the Nasdaq fell 5.52% to 24,315.00, its worst day since April 2025, and the Dow lost 1,833 points (CNBC, Fox Business). Chips led Friday's recovery, with the semiconductor index up 4.2% per Fox Business.

Thursday's rout came as investors weighed what Democratic control of Congress means for AI regulation and data center growth. Qualcomm added to it with a forecast that missed estimates, and Nvidia fell more than 9% (CNBC). Nvidia rose 2.78% Friday to $186.64. Tesla gained 4.23% on the rebound, even as CNBC reported that Scottish Mortgage sold its remaining Tesla stake.

The jobs report added a second pressure point. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October and unemployment fell to 4.1%, far above economists' forecasts, with hourly earnings up 3.1% from a year ago (Fox Business, Axios). Traders see roughly a three-in-four chance of a Fed rate hike on Dec. 9 (CNBC, Axios), though Axios says the report was not a game-changer.

CNBC's week-ahead piece says CPI is expected to show 3.9% annual inflation, up from 3.7%. One strategist said it could take another week before tech hits bottom, while others call the AI trade a discount.
stories.flag: Forecast figures for payrolls differ by source (LSEG versus Dow Jones consensus), and Fed hike odds ranged from about 70% to 77% across reports.
facts: Nasdaq +1.09% on Friday after -5.52% on Thursday.
The Dow fell 0.46% Friday to 51,285.73.
Nvidia fell more than 9% Thursday and rose 2.78% Friday.
October payrolls rose 165,000; unemployment 4.1%.
Fed hike odds for Dec. 9 are roughly 70-77% in CME-based reports.
stories.why: The selloff showed how much of the market rests on the AI buildout, and politics can now move it. A strong jobs report and rising rate-hike odds mean a market already on edge has less support from the Fed. Next week's CPI and Anthropic's IPO roadshow will test whether buyers return.
stories.next: CPI next week, Fed meeting Dec. 8-9, and Nvidia earnings Nov. 17 after the close.

stories.title: Agility's Digit 5 is redesigned around working safely beside people
stories.summary: The humanoid robot adds safety-rated sensors and dedicated safety computers so it can work without cages.
story: IEEE Spectrum reports that Agility Robotics redesigned its Digit humanoid warehouse robot, Digit 5, with safety as a primary goal. Earlier Digit units worked in restricted areas separated from workers by physical panels or laser barriers. Agility says caging robots limited their usefulness, so the new design targets work around people without barriers.

That goal shaped the leg and body shape, safety-rated sensors and dedicated safety computers, according to Spectrum. For falls, the aim is to avoid landing on people by autonomously avoiding, stopping or assuming a seated position. Reports give a 23 kg lifting capacity.

Agility has had to meet industrial safety certification requirements to operate inside customer facilities, per a separate Spectrum piece on humanoid robot safety. The company's CEO has framed it as a design problem, saying a robot cannot be built first and made safe afterward.
MIT Technology Review has argued that humanoids need their own safety rules, since existing standards were written for fixed industrial robots and not for machines that walk among workers.
stories.flag: Independent safety test results and a Digit 5 release date were not found; specifications come from the company and trade press.
facts: Digit 5 was redesigned with safety as a primary goal.
It uses safety-rated sensors and dedicated safety computers.
Fall handling aims to avoid, stop or sit before hitting people.
Reported lifting capacity is 23 kg.
Earlier Digit units worked behind barriers.
stories.why: Humanoids only pay off if they can share space with people, and certification is the gate. A design that passes industrial safety review would show humanoids can move from pilots to routine warehouse work. Standards for walking robots are still being written.
stories.next: Watch for customer deployments and any published safety certification of Digit 5.

stories.title: Two Nature studies use ancient DNA to trace how Celtic and Germanic languages spread
stories.summary: Researchers analyzed thousands of ancient genomes to test where the language families came from and how they moved.
story: Nature published two studies in early November that use ancient genomes to trace the spread of Celtic and Germanic languages, according to Nature's news coverage. Together they analyze more than 4,700 ancient genomes.

The Celtic study uses genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient people to test competing models for where Celtic originated and how it spread. The excerpts available to me do not state its conclusions. The Germanic work follows the language group from its arrival in Scandinavia about 4,000 years ago through its later diversification.

After the Late Iron Age breakup of Germanic into descendant languages, the work finds a southward movement from southern Scandinavia into presumed Celtic-speaking areas, including present-day Germany, Poland and the Netherlands, by about 1,650 years ago. Co-author Guus Kroonen of Leiden University calls DNA a good tracer dye for Germanic spread.

Researchers warn about the limits. Languages can spread without migration, and Dan Bradley of Trinity College Dublin cautioned that tying a language to DNA is tricky. Earlier genomic work had pointed to a Central European origin for Celtic.
stories.flag: The Celtic study's headline findings were not available in the material I could read.
facts: Two Nature studies appeared in early November 2026.
They analyze more than 4,700 ancient genomes together.
The Celtic study uses 4,587 ancient individuals.
Germanic reached Scandinavia about 4,000 years ago.
Researchers caution that languages can spread without migration.
stories.why: Language history has long relied on linguistics and archaeology. Ancient DNA at this scale can test those models directly, though it only shows who moved, not what they spoke. These results will shape debates about how identity and language relate.
stories.next: Watch for responses from linguists and for the Celtic paper's detailed findings.

stories.title: Anthropic's IPO meets data center backlash as valuation hopes fall
stories.summary: Investors now see $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from $2 trillion, with the roadshow expected next week.
story: CNBC reports that investors are bracing for a lower Anthropic valuation, calling $1.5 trillion a stretch. Some now expect $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion, and Bloomberg, cited by Axios, reported a range of $1.1 trillion to $1.3 trillion. The target had been $2 trillion when the company filed confidentially. Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq under ANT, and the roadshow is expected to start next week.

The reason is the tech selloff and midterm politics. CNBC says voters opposed data center ballot measures in 40 of 41 cases, and Democrats won both chambers. Kalshi traders cut the odds of an IPO announcement before December. Anthropic's prospectus already flags the risk, saying opposition to data center development has become more organized and its profile may draw attention to its projects.

The filing also shows about $895.4 billion in committed spending, substantially all of it on compute and infrastructure. Anthropic raised $65 billion at a $965 billion valuation in May, per CNBC. A Gallup survey from May found seven in 10 Americans opposed AI data center construction in their area.

Analysts split on what scrutiny means. Georgetown's Reena Aggarwal said AI is so hot-button that Anthropic will be in the spotlight, while Renaissance Capital's Matt Kennedy said public markets force more transparency. Anthropic declined to comment to CNBC.
stories.flag: Valuation ranges are investor estimates, not a price, and the pricing date has not been announced.
facts: Investors now see $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion versus an earlier $2 trillion target.
The planned ticker is ANT on Nasdaq.
The roadshow is expected to start next week.
The filing shows about $895.4 billion in compute commitments.
Voters opposed data center ballot measures in 40 of 41 cases, per CNBC.
stories.why: Anthropic is the biggest test of whether public markets will fund the AI buildout. A lower valuation would signal investors are pricing in political and compute risk. The outcome will affect how other AI companies raise money.
stories.next: Roadshow expected next week, with a mid-November debut reported by CNBC.

stories.title: AI agents run an automated Shanghai lab that synthesizes and sequences DNA
stories.summary: A Nature paper describes a lab built around AI agents that ran more than 11,000 steps with humans only restocking supplies.
story: Nature reports on an AI-native laboratory at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, which a Nature paper calls an experimental lab for autonomous biomolecular operations. Robotic arms move samples between more than 20 instrument types, and a team of AI agents designs and runs experiments from a simple human prompt.

According to the paper, the system ran over 11,000 steps across DNA synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing. Humans handled only hardware maintenance, such as restocking reagents and labware. A robotic arm with dual-camera machine vision operates a Nanopore sequencer, and the team redesigned its flow cell cover so the arm could grip it.

The team tested it by detecting a cancer-linked mutation in a DNA sample and by encoding a message in DNA using the four nucleotide bases. The researchers designed the lab around AI from the start rather than adding AI to an existing facility.
Nature's coverage frames this as part of a wider push for AI co-scientists. The sources I found do not give error rates or comparisons with human-run labs.
stories.flag: Error rates, cost and comparisons with human-run labs were not found in the coverage.
facts: The lab is at Shanghai Jiao Tong University.
It operates more than 20 types of instrument.
It ran over 11,000 steps in one paper's experiments.
Humans only restocked supplies and maintained hardware.
Tests included detecting a cancer-linked mutation and encoding a message in DNA.
stories.why: This is a concrete example of agents doing physical lab work end to end. If it scales, experiment design could move from weeks of human planning to a prompt. The open questions are reliability, oversight and safety for biology workflows.
stories.next: Watch for independent replication and for other labs adopting similar agent-run setups.

briefs: Nature reports hundreds of roughly 26,000-year-old engravings in Spain's Cova de la Font Major, a cave tourists often visit, with some that appear to use natural fissures for animation (Nature).
Anthropic began rolling out a read-only Personal Finance beta for Pro, Max and Ultra users in the US, linking accounts through Plaid (TechCrunch).
The Regional Transit Measure was winning with about 61% yes across the Bay Area, KQED's tally showed 61.8%, and nearly 65% of Alameda County's share would go to BART operations (KQED).
OpenAI's CFO said the company launched GPT-6 Cyber on Thursday, a company statement not yet independently detailed (CNBC).
